metadata.title: New normal subgroups for the group representation of the Cayley tree.

nodes.name: Cayley tree (Bethe lattice) $\Gamma^k$
nodes.statement: A Cayley tree (Bethe lattice) $\Gamma^k$ of order $k\geq 1$ is an infinite homogeneous tree, i.e., a graph without cycles, such that exactly $k+1$ edges originate from each vertex. Let $\Gamma^k=(V,L)$ where $V$ is the set of vertices and $L$ that of edges (arcs).
nodes.statement_short: An infinite cycle-free homogeneous tree $\Gamma^k=(V,L)$ with exactly $k+1$ edges at every vertex.
differentia: exactly $k+1$ edges originate from each vertex

nodes.name: A group representation of the Cayley tree, $G_{k}$
nodes.statement: Let $G_{k}$ be a free product of $k+1$ cyclic groups of the second order with generators $a_{1},a_{2},...a_{k+1},$ respectively.
nodes.genus: a free product of $k+1$ cyclic groups of the second order

nodes.name: One-to-one correspondence between $V$ and $G_{k}$
nodes.statement: It is known that there exists a one to one correspondence between the set of vertices $V$ of the Cayley tree $\Gamma^{k}$ and the group $G_{k}$.
nodes.statement_short: The vertex set of $\Gamma^k$ can be identified bijectively with the group $G_k$.
assumptions: A Cayley tree (Bethe lattice) $\Gamma^k$ of order $k\geq 1$
Let $G_{k}$ be a free product of $k+1$ cyclic groups of the second order with generators $a_{1},a_{2},...a_{k+1},$ respectively.
conclusions: there exists a one to one correspondence between the set of vertices $V$ of the Cayley tree $\Gamma^{k}$ and the group $G_{k}$

nodes.name: Construction of the vertex-group correspondence
nodes.statement: To give this correspondence we fix an arbitrary element $x_{0}\in V$ and let it correspond to the unit element $e$ of the group $G_{k}.$ Using $a_{1},...,a_{k+1}$ we numerate the nearest-neighbors of element $e$, moving by positive direction. Now we'll give numeration of the nearest-neighbors of each $a_{i}, i=1,...,k+1$ by $a_{i}a_{j}, j=1,...,k+1$. Since all $a_{i}$ have the common neighbor $e$ we give to it $a_{i}a_{i}=a_{i}^{2}=e.$ Other neighbor are numerated starting from $a_{i}a_{i}$ by the positive direction. We numerate the set of all the nearest-neighbors of each $a_{i}a_{j}$ by words $a_{i}a_{j}a_{q}, q=1,...,k+1,$ starting from $a_{i}a_{j}a_{j}=a_{i}$ by the positive direction. Iterating this argument one gets a one-to-one correspondence between the set of vertices $V$ of the Cayley tree $\Gamma^{k}$ and the group $G_{k}.$
nodes.statement_short: Explicit construction: anchor $x_0$ at $e$, then numerate nearest-neighbours level by level with words in the generators.

nodes.name: Anchor a base vertex at the identity
nodes.statement: To give this correspondence we fix an arbitrary element $x_{0}\in V$ and let it correspond to the unit element $e$ of the group $G_{k}.$
nodes.statement_short: Fix a root vertex and send it to $e$.

nodes.name: Numerate the neighbours of $e$
nodes.statement: Using $a_{1},...,a_{k+1}$ we numerate the nearest-neighbors of element $e$, moving by positive direction.
nodes.statement_short: Label the $k+1$ neighbours of the root by the generators.

nodes.name: Numerate the neighbours of each $a_{i}$
nodes.statement: Now we'll give numeration of the nearest-neighbors of each $a_{i}, i=1,...,k+1$ by $a_{i}a_{j}, j=1,...,k+1$. Since all $a_{i}$ have the common neighbor $e$ we give to it $a_{i}a_{i}=a_{i}^{2}=e.$ Other neighbor are numerated starting from $a_{i}a_{i}$ by the positive direction.
nodes.statement_short: Label second-level vertices by two-letter words, using $a_i^2=e$ to recover the root.

nodes.name: Numerate the neighbours of each $a_{i}a_{j}$
nodes.statement: We numerate the set of all the nearest-neighbors of each $a_{i}a_{j}$ by words $a_{i}a_{j}a_{q}, q=1,...,k+1,$ starting from $a_{i}a_{j}a_{j}=a_{i}$ by the positive direction.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the labelling to three-letter words.

nodes.name: Iterate to obtain the bijection
nodes.statement: Iterating this argument one gets a one-to-one correspondence between the set of vertices $V$ of the Cayley tree $\Gamma^{k}$ and the group $G_{k}.$
nodes.statement_short: Iterating the labelling yields the required bijection.

nodes.name: Length $l(x)$ of a word $x\in G_{k}$
nodes.statement: Any(minimal represented) element $x\in G_{k}$ has the following form: \,\ $x=a_{i_{1}}a_{i_{2}}...a_{i_{n}},$ where $1\leq i_{m}\leq k+1, m=1,...,n.$ The number $n$ is called the length of the word $x$ and is denoted by $l(x).$
nodes.statement_short: The length $l(x)$ of $x\in G_k$ is the number of generators in its minimal word representation.

nodes.name: $w_{x}(a_{i})$, the number of occurrences of $a_{i}$ in $x$
nodes.statement: The number of letters $a_{i}, i=1,...,k+1,$ that enter the non-contractible representation of the word $x$ is denoted by $w_{x}(a_{i}).$
differentia: that enter the non-contractible representation of the word $x$

nodes.name: Proposition 1 (kernel of a homomorphism of $G_{k}$; index equals order of image)
nodes.statement: \cite{2} \ Let $\varphi$ be homomorphism of the group $G_{k}$ with the kernel $H.$ Then $H$ is a normal subgroup of the group $G_{k}$ and $\varphi(G_{k})\simeq G_{k}/H,$ (where $G_{k}/H$ is a quotient group) i.e., the index $|G_{k}:H|$ coincides with the order $|\varphi(G_{k})|$ of the group $\varphi(G_{k}).$
nodes.statement_short: The kernel of a homomorphism of $G_k$ is normal, and its index equals the order of the image.
assumptions: Let $\varphi$ be homomorphism of the group $G_{k}$ with the kernel $H.$
conclusions: $H$ is a normal subgroup of the group $G_{k}$ and $\varphi(G_{k})\simeq G_{k}/H,$ (where $G_{k}/H$ is a quotient group)
the index $|G_{k}:H|$ coincides with the order $|\varphi(G_{k})|$ of the group $\varphi(G_{k}).$

nodes.name: Natural homomorphism onto the quotient group
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a normal subgroup of a group $G$. Natural homomorphism $g$ from $G$ onto the quotient group $G/H$ by the formula $g(a)=aH$ for all $a\in G.$ Then $Ker\varphi=H.$
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, every normal subgroup $H$ is the kernel of the natural map $G\to G/H$.

nodes.name: Contractible intersection
nodes.statement: Let $M_{1}, M_{2},..., M_{m}$ be some sets and $M_{i}\neq M_{j},$ for $i\neq j.$ We call the intersection $\cap_{i=1}^{m}M_{i}$ contractible if there exists $i_{0} (1\leq i_{0}\leq m)$ such that $$\cap_{i=1}^{m}M_{i}=\left(\cap_{i=1}^{i_{0}-1}M_{i}\right)\cap\left(\cap_{i=i_{0}+1}^{m}M_{i}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: An intersection is contractible when one of its members can be dropped without changing it.
differentia: there exists $i_{0} (1\leq i_{0}\leq m)$ such that $$\cap_{i=1}^{m}M_{i}=\left(\cap_{i=1}^{i_{0}-1}M_{i}\right)\cap\left(\cap_{i=i_{0}+1}^{m}M_{i}\right).$$

nodes.name: The subgroup $H_{A}$
nodes.statement: Put \begin{equation} H_{A}=\left\{x\in G_{k}\,\ | \,\ \sum_{i\in A}\omega_{x}(a_{i}) \ {\it is \ even} \right\},\ \ A\subset N_{k}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $H_{A}$ collects the words whose total number of letters indexed by $A$ is even.

nodes.name: Proposition 2 (properties of $H_{A}$ and of non-contractible intersections)
nodes.statement:
\cite{5} For any $\emptyset 
eq A \subseteq N_{k},$ the set $H_{A}\subset G_{k}$ satisfies the following properties: (a) $H_{A}$ is a normal subgroup and $|G_{k}:H_{A}|=2;$\ (b) $H_{A}
eq H_{B}$,\ for all $A
eq B \subseteq N_{k};$\ (c) Let $A_{1}, A_{2},...,A_{m}\subseteq N_{k}.$ If $\cap_{i=1}^{m}H_{A_{i}}$ is non-contractible, then it is a normal subgroup of index $2^{m}.$
nodes.statement_short: Each $H_A$ is a distinct index-2 normal subgroup, and a non-contractible intersection of $m$ of them has index $2^m$.
conclusions: then it is a normal subgroup of index $2^{m}.$

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (no normal subgroups of odd index; normal subgroups of every even index)
nodes.statement: \cite{5} \item 1. The group $G_{k}$ does not have normal subgroups of odd index $(\neq 1)$. \item 2. The group $G_{k}$ has a normal subgroups of arbitrary even index.
nodes.statement_short: $G_k$ has no normal subgroup of odd index $\neq 1$, but has one of every even index.
conclusions: 1. The group $G_{k}$ does not have normal subgroups of odd index $(\neq 1)$.
2. The group $G_{k}$ has a normal subgroups of arbitrary even index.

nodes.name: Dihedral group of degree $4$ ($D_{4}$)
nodes.statement: A group $G$ is called a \textbf{dihedral} group of degree $4$ $(i.e.,D_{4})$ if $G$ is generated by two elements $a$ and $b$ satisfying the relations $$o(a)=4, \ o(b)=2, \ ba=a^{3}b.$$
differentia: $G$ is generated by two elements $a$ and $b$ satisfying the relations $$o(a)=4, \ o(b)=2, \ ba=a^{3}b.$$

nodes.name: Quaternion group ($Q_{8}$)
nodes.statement: A group $G$ is called a \textbf{quaternion} group $(i.e., Q_{8})$ if $G$ is generated by two elements $a,\ b$ satisfying the relation $$o(a)=4, a^{2}=b^{2}, ba=a^{3}b.$$
differentia: $G$ is generated by two elements $a,\ b$ satisfying the relation $$o(a)=4, a^{2}=b^{2}, ba=a^{3}b.$$

nodes.name: $D_{4}$ is not isomorphic to $Q_{8}$
nodes.statement: \emph{\cite{2}} $D_{4}$ is not isomorph to $Q_{8}.$

nodes.name: Klein 8-group ($K_{8}$)
nodes.statement: A commutative group $G$ is called a \textbf{Klein 8-group} $(i.e.,K_{8})$ if $G$ is generated by three elements $a, b$ and $c$ satisfying the relations $o(a)=o(b)=o(c)=2.$
differentia: $G$ is generated by three elements $a, b$ and $c$ satisfying the relations $o(a)=o(b)=o(c)=2.$

nodes.name: Proposition 3 (only two noncommutative groups of order $8$)
nodes.statement: \emph{\cite{2}} There exist (up to isomorphism) only two noncommutative nonisomorphic groups of order $8$
conclusions: There exist (up to isomorphism) only two noncommutative nonisomorphic groups of order $8$

nodes.name: Proposition 4 (image of $G_{k}$ of order 8 is $D_{4}$ or $K_{8}$)
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi$ is a homomorphism of the group $G_{k}$ onto a group $G$ of order 8. Then $\varphi(G_{k})$ is isomorph to either $D_{4}$ or $K_{8}.$
nodes.statement_short: Any order-8 epimorphic image of $G_k$ is either $D_4$ or the Klein 8-group.
assumptions: Let $\varphi$ is a homomorphism of the group $G_{k}$ onto a group $G$ of order 8.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement: \texttt{Case 1} Let $\varphi(G_{k})$ is isomorph to any noncommutative group of order $8$. By Proposition \ref{p1} $\varphi(G_{k})$ is isomorph to either $D_{4}$ or $Q_{8}.$ Let $\varphi(G_{k})\simeq Q_{8}$ and $e_{q}$ is an identity element of the group $Q_{8}$. Then $e_{q}=\varphi(e)=\varphi(a_{i}^{2})=(\varphi(a_{i}))^{2}$ where $a_{i}\in G_{k}, \,\ i\in N_{k}.$ Hence for the order of $\varphi(a_{i})$ we have $o(\varphi(a_{i}))\in \{1,2\}.$ It is easy to check there are only two elements of the group $Q_{8}$ which order of element less than two. This is contradict. \texttt{Case 2} \ Let $\varphi(G_{k},\ast)$ is isomorph to any commutative group $(G,\ast_{1})$ of order $8$. Then there exist distinct elements $a,b \in G$ such that $o(a)=o(b)=2.$ Let $H=\{e,a,b,ab\}.$ It's easy to check that $(H ,\ast_{1})$ is a normal subgroup of the group $(G,\ast_{1}).$ For $c\notin H$ we have $H\neq cH \ (cH=c\ast_{1}H).$ Hence $\varphi(G_{k},\ast)$ is isomorph to only one commutative group $(cH\cup H,\ast_{1}).$ Clearly $(cH\cup H,\ast_{1})\simeq K_{8}.$
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis: $Q_{8}$ is impossible because every $\varphi(a_{i})$ has order $\le 2$, and the commutative case forces $K_{8}$.

nodes.name: Case 1: noncommutative image, $Q_{8}$ excluded
nodes.statement: \texttt{Case 1} Let $\varphi(G_{k})$ is isomorph to any noncommutative group of order $8$. By Proposition \ref{p1} $\varphi(G_{k})$ is isomorph to either $D_{4}$ or $Q_{8}.$ Let $\varphi(G_{k})\simeq Q_{8}$ and $e_{q}$ is an identity element of the group $Q_{8}$. Then $e_{q}=\varphi(e)=\varphi(a_{i}^{2})=(\varphi(a_{i}))^{2}$ where $a_{i}\in G_{k}, \,\ i\in N_{k}.$ Hence for the order of $\varphi(a_{i})$ we have $o(\varphi(a_{i}))\in \{1,2\}.$ It is easy to check there are only two elements of the group $Q_{8}$ which order of element less than two. This is contradict.
nodes.statement_short: Rule out $Q_{8}$: generators of $G_k$ are involutions, but $Q_8$ has too few elements of order $\le 2$.

nodes.name: Case 2: commutative image is $K_{8}$
nodes.statement: \texttt{Case 2} \ Let $\varphi(G_{k},\ast)$ is isomorph to any commutative group $(G,\ast_{1})$ of order $8$. Then there exist distinct elements $a,b \in G$ such that $o(a)=o(b)=2.$ Let $H=\{e,a,b,ab\}.$ It's easy to check that $(H ,\ast_{1})$ is a normal subgroup of the group $(G,\ast_{1}).$ For $c\notin H$ we have $H\neq cH \ (cH=c\ast_{1}H).$ Hence $\varphi(G_{k},\ast)$ is isomorph to only one commutative group $(cH\cup H,\ast_{1}).$ Clearly $(cH\cup H,\ast_{1})\simeq K_{8}.$
nodes.statement_short: In the commutative case, a Klein 4-subgroup plus one coset exhausts $G$, giving $K_{8}$.

nodes.name: Minimal set of order-two generators $b_{1},...,b_{r}$ of $G$
nodes.statement: The group $G$ has a finitely generators of the order two and $r$ is a minimal number of such generators of the group $G$ and without loss of generality we can take these generators are $b_{1},b_{2},...b_{r}.$ Let $e_{1}$ is an identity element of the group $G.$ We define homomorphism from $G_{k}$ onto $G.$
nodes.statement_short: Assume $G$ is generated by a minimal set of $r$ involutions $b_1,\dots,b_r$, with identity $e_1$.

nodes.name: The map $u_{n}$ on generators
nodes.statement: Let $\Xi_{n}=\{A_{1}, \,\ A_{2},...,A_{n}\}$ be a partition of $N_{k}\backslash A_{0}, \,\ 0\leq|A_{0}|\leq k+1-n.$ Then we consider homomorphism $u_{n}:\{a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{k+1}\}\rightarrow \{e_{1}, b_{1}...,b_{m}\}$ as\\ \begin{equation} u_{n}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} e_{1}, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ x=a_{i}, i\in A_{0}\\[2.5mm] b_{j}, \ \mbox{if}\ \ x=a_{i}, i\in A_{j}, j=\overline{1,n}. \\ \end{array}\right.\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Given a partition $\Xi_n$ of $N_k\setminus A_0$, $u_n$ sends generators indexed by $A_0$ to $e_1$ and those indexed by $A_j$ to $b_j$.

nodes.name: Representation $R_{b}[b_{1},b_{2},...,b_{m}]$ of a word
nodes.statement: For $b\in G$ we denote $R_{b}[ b_{1}, b_{2}, ..., b_{m}]$ is a representation of the word $b$ by generators $b_{1}, b_{2}, ..., b_{r}, \ r\leq m.$
differentia: by generators $b_{1}, b_{2}, ..., b_{r}, \ r\leq m.$

nodes.name: The homomorphism $\gamma_{n}: G\rightarrow G$
nodes.statement: Define the homomorphism $\gamma_{n}: G\rightarrow G$ by the formula\\ \begin{equation}\gamma_{n}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} e_{1}, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ x=e_{1}\\[2.5mm] b_{i}, \ \mbox{if}\ \ x=b_{i}, i=\overline{1,r}\\[2.5mm] R_{b_{i}}[b_{1},...,b_{r}], \ \mbox{if}\ \ x=b_{i}, i\neq \overline{1,r}\\ \end{array}\right.\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma_n$ fixes the minimal generators and rewrites every other element by its representation in them.

nodes.name: The set $H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)$
nodes.statement: Put\\ \begin{equation} H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)=\{x\in G_{k}|\,\ l(\gamma_{n}(u_{n}(x))):2p\},\ 2\leq n \leq k-1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $H^{(p)}_{\Xi_n}(G)$ collects the $x\in G_k$ whose image length under $\gamma_n\circ u_n$ is divisible by $2p$.

nodes.name: The reduced word $\tilde{x}$ and the equivalence relation $x\sim y$
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma_{n}(u_{n}(x)))=\tilde{x}.$ We introduce the following equivalence relation on the set $G_{k}:$ $x\sim y$ if $\tilde{x}=\tilde{y}.$ It's easy to check this relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\tilde{x}=\gamma_n(u_n(x))$ and declare $x\sim y$ when $\tilde{x}=\tilde{y}$.

nodes.name: Proposition 5 ($H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{p}}(G)$ is normal of index $2p$)
nodes.statement: Let \ $\Xi_{n}=\{A_{1}, A_{2},...,A_{n}\}$ be a partition of $N_{k}\backslash A_{0}, \,\ 0\leq|A_{0}|\leq k+1-n.$ Then $H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{p}}(G)$ is a normal subgroup of index $2p$ of the group $G_{k}.$
nodes.statement_short: For any admissible partition $\Xi_n$, the set $H^{(p)}_{\Xi_p}(G)$ is a normal subgroup of $G_k$ of index $2p$.
assumptions: Let \ $\Xi_{n}=\{A_{1}, A_{2},...,A_{n}\}$ be a partition of $N_{k}\backslash A_{0}, \,\ 0\leq|A_{0}|\leq k+1-n.$
conclusions: $H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{p}}(G)$ is a normal subgroup of index $2p$ of the group $G_{k}.$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement: For $x=a_{i_{1}}a_{i_{2}}...a_{i_{n}}\in G_{k}$ it's sufficient to show that $x^{-1}H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)$ $x\subseteq H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G).$ Suppose that there exist $y\in G_{k}$ such that $l(\tilde{y})\geq 2p.$ Let $\tilde{y}=b_{i_{1}}b_{i_{2}}...b_{i_{q}}, \ q\geq 2p$ and $S=\{b_{i_{1}}, b_{i_{1}}b_{i_{2}},..., b_{i_{1}}b_{i_{2}}...b_{i_{q}}\}.$ Since $S\subseteq G$ there exist $x_{1}, x_{2} \in S$ such that $x_{1}=x_{2}.$ But this is contradict to $\tilde{y}$ is a non-contractible. Thus we have proved that $l(\tilde{y})<2p.$ Hence for any $x\in H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)$ we have $\tilde{x}=e_{1}.$ Now we take any element $z$ from the set $x^{-1}H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)\ x.$ Then $z=x^{-1}h\ x$ for some $h\in H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G).$ We have $\tilde{z}=\gamma_{n}(v_{n}(z))=\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x^{-1}h\ x)\right)=$ $=\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x^{-1})v_{n}(h)v_{n}(x)\right)= \gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x^{-1})\right)\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(h)\right)\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x)\right).$ From $\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(h)\right)=e_{1}$ we get $\tilde{z}=e_{1}$ i.e., $z\in H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G).$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Show conjugation-invariance: pigeonhole forces $l(\tilde{y})<2p$, hence $\tilde{x}=e_{1}$ on $H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)$, and multiplicativity of $\gamma_{n}\circ u_{n}$ gives $\tilde{z}=e_{1}$.

nodes.name: Reduce to conjugation-invariance
nodes.statement: For $x=a_{i_{1}}a_{i_{2}}...a_{i_{n}}\in G_{k}$ it's sufficient to show that $x^{-1}H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)$ $x\subseteq H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G).$
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove $x^{-1}H^{(p)}_{\Xi_n}(G)x\subseteq H^{(p)}_{\Xi_n}(G)$.

nodes.name: Contradiction from a long reduced word
nodes.statement: Suppose that there exist $y\in G_{k}$ such that $l(\tilde{y})\geq 2p.$ Let $\tilde{y}=b_{i_{1}}b_{i_{2}}...b_{i_{q}}, \ q\geq 2p$ and $S=\{b_{i_{1}}, b_{i_{1}}b_{i_{2}},..., b_{i_{1}}b_{i_{2}}...b_{i_{q}}\}.$ Since $S\subseteq G$ there exist $x_{1}, x_{2} \in S$ such that $x_{1}=x_{2}.$ But this is contradict to $\tilde{y}$ is a non-contractible.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $l(\tilde{y})\ge 2p$; pigeonhole on prefixes yields a coincidence contradicting non-contractibility.

nodes.name: Consequence: $\tilde{x}=e_{1}$ on the subgroup
nodes.statement: Thus we have proved that $l(\tilde{y})<2p.$ Hence for any $x\in H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)$ we have $\tilde{x}=e_{1}.$
nodes.statement_short: Deduce $l(\tilde{y})<2p$, so every member of $H^{(p)}_{\Xi_n}(G)$ has $\tilde{x}=e_1$.

nodes.name: Conjugates stay in the subgroup
nodes.statement: Now we take any element $z$ from the set $x^{-1}H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G)\ x.$ Then $z=x^{-1}h\ x$ for some $h\in H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G).$ We have $\tilde{z}=\gamma_{n}(v_{n}(z))=\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x^{-1}h\ x)\right)=$ $=\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x^{-1})v_{n}(h)v_{n}(x)\right)= \gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x^{-1})\right)\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(h)\right)\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(x)\right).$ From $\gamma_{n}\left(v_{n}(h)\right)=e_{1}$ we get $\tilde{z}=e_{1}$ i.e., $z\in H^{(p)}_{\Xi_{n}}(G).$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\tilde{z}$ multiplicatively and use $\gamma_n(v_n(h))=e_1$ to conclude $z$ lies in the subgroup.

nodes.name: The family $\Re$ of triple intersections
nodes.statement: For $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\subset N_{k}$ and $\cap_{i=1}^{3}H_{A_{i}}$ is non-contractible we denote following set\\ $$\Re=\{\cap_{i=1}^{3}H_{A_{i}}| \ A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\subset N_{k}\}$$
nodes.statement_short: $\Re$ is the family of non-contractible triple intersections $H_{A_1}\cap H_{A_2}\cap H_{A_3}$.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (description of all normal subgroups of index 8 of $G_{k}$)
nodes.statement: For the group $G_{k}$ following statement is hold\\ $$\{H|\ H \ is\ a\ normal\ subgroup\ of\ G_{k}\ with\ |G_{k}:H|=8\}=$$ $$=\{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\} \cup \Re.$$
nodes.statement_short: The normal subgroups of index 8 in $G_k$ are exactly the $D_4$-type subgroups $H^{(4)}_{C_0C_1C_2}(D_4)$ together with the family $\Re$.
conclusions: $$\{H|\ H \ is\ a\ normal\ subgroup\ of\ G_{k}\ with\ |G_{k}:H|=8\}=$$ $$=\{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\} \cup \Re.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be a homomorphism with $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=8.$ Then by Proposition 2 we have $\phi(G_{k})\simeq K_{8}$ and $\phi(G_{k})\simeq D_{4}.$ Let $\phi:G_{k}\rightarrow K_{8}$ be an epimorphism. For any nonempty sets $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\subset N_{k}$ we give one to one correspondence between $\{Ker\phi| \ \phi(G_{k})\simeq K_{8}\}$ and $\Re.$ Let $a_{i}\in G_{k}, i\in N_{k}.$ We define following homomorphism corresponding to the set $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}.$ $$\phi_{A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}}(a_{i})=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} a, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{1}\setminus(A_{2}\cup A_{3})\\[2.5mm] b, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{2}\setminus(A_{1}\cup A_{3})\\[2.5mm] c, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{3}\setminus(A_{1}\cup A_{2})\\[2.5mm] ab, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in (A_{1}\cap A_{2})\setminus(A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3})\\[2.5mm] ac, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in (A_{1}\cap A_{3})\setminus(A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3})\\[2.5mm] bc, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in (A_{2}\cap A_{3})\setminus(A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3})\\[2.5mm] abc, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3}\\[2.5mm] e, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in N_{k}\setminus(A_{1}\cup A_{2}\cup A_{3}). \\ \end{array}\right.$$ If $i\in \emptyset$ then we'll accept that there is not any index $i\in N_{k}$ which that condition is not satisfied. It is easy to check $Ker \phi_{A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}}=H_{A_{1}}\cap H_{A_{2}}\cap H_{A_{3}}.$ Hence $\{Ker\phi| \ \phi(G_{k})\simeq K_{8}\}=\Re.$ Now we'll consider the case $\phi(G_{k})\simeq D_{4}.$ Let $\phi: G_{k}\rightarrow D_{4}$ be epimorphisms. Put\\ $$C_{0}=\{i| \ \phi(a_{i})=e\}, \ \ C_{1}=\{i| \ \phi(a_{i})=b\},\ C_{2}=\{i| \ \phi(a_{i})=ab\}$$ One can construct following homomorphism (corresponding to $C_{0}, C_{1}, C_{2}$)\\ $$\phi_{C_{0} C_{1} C_{2}}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} e, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=e\\[2.5mm] a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a^{2}, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a^{3}, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}\\[2.5mm] b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1} \\[2.5mm] ab, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a^{2}b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a^{3}b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}. \\ \end{array}\right.$$ Straight away we conclude $Ker(\phi_{C_{0} C_{1} C_{2}})=H^{(4)}_{C_{0} C_{1} C_{2}}(D_{4}).$ We have constructed all homomorphisms $\phi$ on the group $G_{k}$ which $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=8.$ Thus by Proposition \ref{p1} one get\\ $$\{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=8\}\subseteq \{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\} \cup \Re.$$\\ By Proposition \ref{p2} and Proposition \ref{p3.} we can see easily\\ $$\Re \cup \{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\}\subseteq \{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=8\}.$$\\ The theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Double inclusion: enumerate all index-8 epimorphisms (onto $K_{8}$, then onto $D_{4}$), identify their kernels with $\Re$ and $H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})$, then invoke Propositions 1, 2 and 5 for the reverse inclusion.

nodes.name: Reduce to the two possible images $K_{8}$ and $D_{4}$
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be a homomorphism with $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=8.$ Then by Proposition 2 we have $\phi(G_{k})\simeq K_{8}$ and $\phi(G_{k})\simeq D_{4}.$
nodes.statement_short: An index-8 kernel forces the image to be $K_{8}$ or $D_{4}$.

nodes.name: Case $\phi(G_{k})\simeq K_{8}$: kernels are exactly $\Re$
nodes.statement: Let $\phi:G_{k}\rightarrow K_{8}$ be an epimorphism. For any nonempty sets $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\subset N_{k}$ we give one to one correspondence between $\{Ker\phi| \ \phi(G_{k})\simeq K_{8}\}$ and $\Re.$ Let $a_{i}\in G_{k}, i\in N_{k}.$ We define following homomorphism corresponding to the set $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}.$ $$\phi_{A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}}(a_{i})=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} a, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{1}\setminus(A_{2}\cup A_{3})\\[2.5mm] b, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{2}\setminus(A_{1}\cup A_{3})\\[2.5mm] c, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{3}\setminus(A_{1}\cup A_{2})\\[2.5mm] ab, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in (A_{1}\cap A_{2})\setminus(A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3})\\[2.5mm] ac, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in (A_{1}\cap A_{3})\setminus(A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3})\\[2.5mm] bc, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in (A_{2}\cap A_{3})\setminus(A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3})\\[2.5mm] abc, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in A_{1}\cap A_{2}\cap A_{3}\\[2.5mm] e, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ i\in N_{k}\setminus(A_{1}\cup A_{2}\cup A_{3}). \\ \end{array}\right.$$ If $i\in \emptyset$ then we'll accept that there is not any index $i\in N_{k}$ which that condition is not satisfied. It is easy to check $Ker \phi_{A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}}=H_{A_{1}}\cap H_{A_{2}}\cap H_{A_{3}}.$ Hence $\{Ker\phi| \ \phi(G_{k})\simeq K_{8}\}=\Re.$
nodes.statement_short: Build the epimorphism $\phi_{A_1A_2A_3}$ onto $K_8$ and check its kernel is $H_{A_1}\cap H_{A_2}\cap H_{A_3}$.

nodes.name: Case $\phi(G_{k})\simeq D_{4}$: kernels are the $H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})$
nodes.statement: Now we'll consider the case $\phi(G_{k})\simeq D_{4}.$ Let $\phi: G_{k}\rightarrow D_{4}$ be epimorphisms. Put\\ $$C_{0}=\{i| \ \phi(a_{i})=e\}, \ \ C_{1}=\{i| \ \phi(a_{i})=b\},\ C_{2}=\{i| \ \phi(a_{i})=ab\}$$ One can construct following homomorphism (corresponding to $C_{0}, C_{1}, C_{2}$)\\ $$\phi_{C_{0} C_{1} C_{2}}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} e, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=e\\[2.5mm] a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a^{2}, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a^{3}, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}\\[2.5mm] b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1} \\[2.5mm] ab, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a^{2}b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a^{3}b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}. \\ \end{array}\right.$$ Straight away we conclude $Ker(\phi_{C_{0} C_{1} C_{2}})=H^{(4)}_{C_{0} C_{1} C_{2}}(D_{4}).$
nodes.statement_short: Build the epimorphism $\phi_{C_0C_1C_2}$ onto $D_4$ from the reduced word $\tilde{x}$ and identify its kernel.

nodes.name: First inclusion via Proposition 1
nodes.statement: We have constructed all homomorphisms $\phi$ on the group $G_{k}$ which $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=8.$ Thus by Proposition \ref{p1} one get\\ $$\{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=8\}\subseteq \{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\} \cup \Re.$$
nodes.statement_short: Since every index-8 normal subgroup is such a kernel, the inclusion $\subseteq$ holds.

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion via Propositions 2 and 5
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p2} and Proposition \ref{p3.} we can see easily\\ $$\Re \cup \{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\}\subseteq \{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=8\}.$$\\ The theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Propositions 2 and 5 give the reverse inclusion, completing the equality.

nodes.name: Corollary 1 (number of normal subgroups of index 8)
nodes.statement: The number of all normal subgroups of index $8$ for the group $G_{k}$ is equal to $8^{k+1}-6\cdot4^{k+1}+3^{k+1}+9\cdot2^{k+1}-5.$
conclusions: The number of all normal subgroups of index $8$ for the group $G_{k}$ is equal to $8^{k+1}-6\cdot4^{k+1}+3^{k+1}+9\cdot2^{k+1}-5.$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: Number of elements of the set $H_{A}\subset G_{k}, \emptyset \neq A\subset N_{k}$ is $2^{k+1}-1.$ Then $|\Re|=(2^{k+1})(2^{k+1}-2)(2^{k+2}-3).$ Let $C_{0}\subset N_{k}$ is a fixed set and $|C_{0}|=p.$ If $C_{1}, C_{2}$ is a partition of $N_{k}\setminus C_{0}$ then there are $2^{k-p+1}-2$ ways to choose the sets $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}.$ Hence the cardinality of $\{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\}$ is equal to\\ $$(2^{k+1}-2)C^{0}_{k+1}+(2^{k}-2)C_{k+1}^{1}+...+2C_{k+1}^{k-1}=3^{k+1}-2^{k+2}+1.$$\\ Since $\Re$ and $\{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})\}|\ C_{1},C_{2}\subset N_{k}$ are disjoint sets, cardinality of the union of these sets is $8^{k+1}-6\cdot4^{k+1}+3^{k+1}+9\cdot2^{k+1}-5.$
nodes.statement_short: Count $|\Re|$ and the number of $D_{4}$-type subgroups by summing over $|C_{0}|=p$, then add the two disjoint families.

nodes.name: Count the family $\Re$
nodes.statement: Number of elements of the set $H_{A}\subset G_{k}, \emptyset \neq A\subset N_{k}$ is $2^{k+1}-1.$ Then $|\Re|=(2^{k+1})(2^{k+1}-2)(2^{k+2}-3).$
nodes.statement_short: There are $2^{k+1}-1$ subgroups $H_A$, giving the stated $|\Re|$.

nodes.name: Count the $D_{4}$-type subgroups
nodes.statement: Let $C_{0}\subset N_{k}$ is a fixed set and $|C_{0}|=p.$ If $C_{1}, C_{2}$ is a partition of $N_{k}\setminus C_{0}$ then there are $2^{k-p+1}-2$ ways to choose the sets $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}.$ Hence the cardinality of $\{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})|\ C_{1},C_{2}\ is\ a\ partition\ of\ N_{k}\setminus C_{0}\}$ is equal to\\ $$(2^{k+1}-2)C^{0}_{k+1}+(2^{k}-2)C_{k+1}^{1}+...+2C_{k+1}^{k-1}=3^{k+1}-2^{k+2}+1.$$
nodes.statement_short: Sum $2^{k-p+1}-2$ over all choices of $C_{0}$ of size $p$ to get $3^{k+1}-2^{k+2}+1$.

nodes.name: Add the two disjoint families
nodes.statement: Since $\Re$ and $\{H^{(4)}_{C_{0}C_{1}C_{2}}(D_{4})\}|\ C_{1},C_{2}\subset N_{k}$ are disjoint sets, cardinality of the union of these sets is $8^{k+1}-6\cdot4^{k+1}+3^{k+1}+9\cdot2^{k+1}-5.$
nodes.statement_short: Disjointness lets the two counts be added.

nodes.name: The group $R_{10}$
nodes.statement: Let the group $R_{10}$ is generated by the permutations $$\pi_{1}=(1,2)(3,4)(5,6), \ \pi_{2}=(2,3)(4,5)$$
nodes.genus: the group generated by the permutations

nodes.name: Proposition 6 (image of $G_{k}$ of order 10 is $R_{10}$)
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi$ is a homomorphism of the group $G_{k}$ onto a group $G$ of order 10. Then $\varphi(G_{k})$ is isomorph to $R_{10}.$
nodes.statement_short: Every order-10 epimorphic image of $G_k$ is isomorphic to $R_{10}$.
assumptions: Let $\varphi$ is a homomorphism of the group $G_{k}$ onto a group $G$ of order 10.

nodes.name: Lagrange's theorem
nodes.statement: by Lagrange's theorem $|G|$ is divide by $|H|$
nodes.statement_short: Subgroup order divides group order.
assumptions: $(H,\ast)$ is a subgroup of the group $(G,\ast),$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement: Let $(G,\ast)$ be a group and $|G|=10.$ Suppose there exist an epimorphism from $G_{k}$ onto $G.$ It is easy to check that there are at least two elements $a,b\in G_{k}$ such that $o(a)=o(b)=2.$ If $a\ast b=b\ast a$ then $(H,\ast)$ is a subgroup of the group $(G,\ast),$ where $H=\{e,a,b,a\ast b\}.$ Then by Lagrange's theorem $|G|$ is divide by $|H|$ but $10$ is not divide by $4.$ Hence $a\ast b\neq b\ast a.$ We have $\{e,a,b,a\ast b,b\ast a\}\subset G$ If $G$ is generated by three elements then there exist an element $c$ such that $c\notin \{e,a,b,a\ast b,b\ast a\}.$ Then the set $\{e,a,b,a\ast b, b\ast a, c,c\ast a, c\ast b, c\ast a\ast b, c\ast b\ast a\}$ must be equal to $G.$ Since $G$ is a group we get $a\ast b\ast a=b$ but from $o(a)=2$ the last equality is equivalent to $a\ast b=b\ast a.$ This is a contradict. Hence by Lagrange is theorem it's easy to see $$G=\{e,a,b,a\ast b, b\ast a, a\ast b\ast a, b\ast a\ast b,a\ast b\ast a\ast b,b\ast a\ast b\ast a,a\ast b\ast a\ast b\ast a\},$$ where $o(a\ast b)=5.$ Namely $G\simeq R_{10}.$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Two involutions must fail to commute (else $4\mid 10$), a third generator also leads to contradiction, so $G$ is the dihedral-type group $R_{10}$ with $o(a\ast b)=5$.

nodes.name: Setup: an order-10 image has two involutions
nodes.statement: Let $(G,\ast)$ be a group and $|G|=10.$ Suppose there exist an epimorphism from $G_{k}$ onto $G.$ It is easy to check that there are at least two elements $a,b\in G_{k}$ such that $o(a)=o(b)=2.$
nodes.statement_short: Assume an epimorphism onto a group of order 10 and pick two elements of order 2.

nodes.name: The two involutions do not commute
nodes.statement: If $a\ast b=b\ast a$ then $(H,\ast)$ is a subgroup of the group $(G,\ast),$ where $H=\{e,a,b,a\ast b\}.$ Then by Lagrange's theorem $|G|$ is divide by $|H|$ but $10$ is not divide by $4.$ Hence $a\ast b\neq b\ast a.$
nodes.statement_short: Commuting involutions would give a subgroup of order 4, contradicting $4\nmid 10$ by Lagrange.

nodes.name: Rule out a third generator
nodes.statement: We have $\{e,a,b,a\ast b,b\ast a\}\subset G$ If $G$ is generated by three elements then there exist an element $c$ such that $c\notin \{e,a,b,a\ast b,b\ast a\}.$ Then the set $\{e,a,b,a\ast b, b\ast a, c,c\ast a, c\ast b, c\ast a\ast b, c\ast b\ast a\}$ must be equal to $G.$ Since $G$ is a group we get $a\ast b\ast a=b$ but from $o(a)=2$ the last equality is equivalent to $a\ast b=b\ast a.$ This is a contradict.
nodes.statement_short: A third generator forces $a\ast b\ast a=b$, i.e. commutativity, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Identify $G$ with $R_{10}$
nodes.statement: Hence by Lagrange is theorem it's easy to see $$G=\{e,a,b,a\ast b, b\ast a, a\ast b\ast a, b\ast a\ast b,a\ast b\ast a\ast b,b\ast a\ast b\ast a,a\ast b\ast a\ast b\ast a\},$$ where $o(a\ast b)=5.$ Namely $G\simeq R_{10}.$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: List the ten elements, note $o(a\ast b)=5$, and conclude $G\simeq R_{10}$.

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (description of all normal subgroups of index 10 of $G_{k}$)
nodes.statement: For the group $G_{k}$ following statement is hold $$\{H|\ |\ H\ is\ a\ normal\ subgroup\ of\ G_{k}\ with\ |G_{k}:H|=10\}=$$ $$=\{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The normal subgroups of index 10 in $G_k$ are exactly the $R_{10}$-type subgroups $H^{(5)}_{B_0B_1B_2}(R_{10})$.
conclusions: $$\{H|\ |\ H\ is\ a\ normal\ subgroup\ of\ G_{k}\ with\ |G_{k}:H|=10\}=$$ $$=\{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be a homomorphism with $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=10.$ By Proposition \ref{p2.1} $\phi(G_{k})\simeq R_{10}$ and by Proposition \ref{p3.} we can see easily $$\{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}\subset \{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=10\}.$$ Let $\varphi: G_{k}\rightarrow R_{10}$ be epimorphisms. Denote\\ $$B_{0}=\{i| \ \varphi(a_{i})=e\}, \ \ B_{1}=\{i| \ \varphi(a_{i})=a,\ B_{2}=\{i| \ \varphi(a_{i})=b\}.$$\\ Then we can show this homomorphism (corresponding to $B_{1},\ B_{2},\ B_{3}$), i.e.,\\ $$\phi_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} e, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=e\\[2.5mm] a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1} \\[2.5mm] b, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}\\[2.5mm] b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] b\ast a\ast b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b\ast a\ast b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2} \\[2.5mm] b\ast a\ast b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b\ast a\ast b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}. \\ \end{array}\right.$$ We have constructed all homomorphisms $\phi$ on the group $G_{k}$ which $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=10.$ Hence\\ $$\{Ker\phi|\ |G_{k}:Ker\phi|=10\}\subset \{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}.$$\\ By Proposition \ref{p1}\\ $$\{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=10\}=\{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}.$$\\ The theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Double inclusion again: Proposition 6 fixes the image as $R_{10}$, Proposition 5 gives one inclusion, the explicit epimorphism $\phi_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}$ gives the other, and Proposition 1 yields equality.

nodes.name: Image is $R_{10}$; first inclusion
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be a homomorphism with $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=10.$ By Proposition \ref{p2.1} $\phi(G_{k})\simeq R_{10}$ and by Proposition \ref{p3.} we can see easily $$\{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}\subset \{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=10\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Propositions 6 and 5 give that every $H^{(5)}_{B_0B_1B_2}(R_{10})$ has index 10.

nodes.name: Construct the epimorphism onto $R_{10}$
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi: G_{k}\rightarrow R_{10}$ be epimorphisms. Denote\\ $$B_{0}=\{i| \ \varphi(a_{i})=e\}, \ \ B_{1}=\{i| \ \varphi(a_{i})=a,\ B_{2}=\{i| \ \varphi(a_{i})=b\}.$$\\ Then we can show this homomorphism (corresponding to $B_{1},\ B_{2},\ B_{3}$), i.e.,\\ $$\phi_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} e, \ \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=e\\[2.5mm] a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1} \\[2.5mm] b, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b, \ \mbox{if} \ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}\\[2.5mm] b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] b\ast a\ast b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b\ast a\ast b, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2} \\[2.5mm] b\ast a\ast b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1} \\[2.5mm] a\ast b\ast a\ast b\ast a, \ \mbox{if}\ \ \tilde{x}=b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}b_{2}b_{1}. \\ \end{array}\right.$$
nodes.statement_short: Define $\phi_{B_0B_1B_2}$ on reduced words $\tilde{x}$ to realise every epimorphism onto $R_{10}$.

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion for kernels
nodes.statement: We have constructed all homomorphisms $\phi$ on the group $G_{k}$ which $|G_{k}:Ker\phi|=10.$ Hence\\ $$\{Ker\phi|\ |G_{k}:Ker\phi|=10\}\subset \{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: All index-10 kernels are of the constructed form.

nodes.name: Conclude equality via Proposition 1
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p1}\\ $$\{H|\ |G_{k}:H|=10\}=\{H^{(5)}_{B_{0}B_{1}B_{2}}(R_{10})|\ B_{1}, B_{2} \ is\ a\ partition\ of\ the\ set\ N_{k}\setminus B_{0}\}.$$\\ The theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 converts the kernel description into the description of all index-10 normal subgroups.

nodes.name: Corollary 2 (number of normal subgroups of index 10)
nodes.statement: The number of all normal subgroups of index $10$ for the group $G_{k}$ is equal to $3^{k+1}-2^{k+2}+1.$
conclusions: The number of all normal subgroups of index $10$ for the group $G_{k}$ is equal to $3^{k+1}-2^{k+2}+1.$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement: To prove this Corollary is similar to proof of Corollary \ref{c1}.
nodes.statement_short: Deferred: the counting argument is the same as for Corollary 1.
